albums.name: Signal & Noise
albums.speaker: maya
albums.notes: A weekly conversation about the software we live with — what works, what doesn't, and why.
albums.profile:
Maya and Tom take one everyday piece of technology each week and pull it apart: who built it, what they were trying to fix, and what it quietly costs the people who use it.

Expect strong opinions, real examples, and very little hype.

episodes.title: Your Files, Your Rules
episodes.notes: Great intro to local-first. Send to Dan.
lines: Welcome to Signal and Noise. I'm Maya Okafor.
And I'm Tom Becker. Today we're talking about who actually owns the files on your phone.
Here's the thing. Most apps keep your data on their server, and you just get to look at it.
Which is fine, until the company shuts down, or changes the price, or loses interest.
Local-first software flips that around. The copy on your device is the real one, and the cloud is just a backup.
And the nice side effect is speed. Nothing waits on a network request before it shows up.
The hard part is sync. Two devices, two edits, one truth. Somebody has to decide who wins.
My rule of thumb: if the app can't explain where your data lives in one sentence, be careful.
That's a good rule. Next week, we look at why every app now wants to be a subscription.
episodes.summary:
Why local-first apps keep the real copy of your data on your own device, and what that costs.

• {2} Most apps keep your data on their server; you only get to view it.
• {4} Local-first flips it: the device copy is real, the cloud is a backup.
• {6} Sync is the hard part — two edits, one truth.

If an app can't say where your data lives in one sentence, be careful.

bookmarks.note: Use this rule in the team review

episodes.title: Everything Is a Subscription Now
lines: Welcome back to Signal and Noise. Maya, how many subscriptions do you pay for right now?
I counted last night. Fourteen. Three of them I'd forgotten about entirely.
That's the business model working exactly as designed.
To be fair, subscriptions pay for real work. Servers cost money every month, forever.
Sure, but a calculator app doesn't run a server. A one-time price would be honest there.
I think the test is simple. Does the app cost the developer money every time I use it?
If yes, a subscription makes sense. If no, it's rent on something you already bought.
And listeners, check your settings tonight. Look for the ones you forgot.
That's the show. See you next week.
episodes.summary:
When a subscription is fair, and when it's rent.

• {1} Maya counts fourteen subscriptions; three were forgotten.
• {3} Servers cost money every month, which is a fair reason to charge monthly.
• {5} The test: does each use cost the developer money?

episodes.title: In Defense of the Settings Screen
lines: This is Signal and Noise. Tom, you wanted a whole episode about settings screens.
I did, and I'm not sorry. The settings screen is where an app tells you what it really thinks of you.
Hide every option, and you're saying the user can't be trusted. Show every option, and you're saying you couldn't decide.
Good defaults, and then a few honest switches that each explain themselves in one line.
I'd add one thing. A switch should take effect right away. No restart, no mystery.
Agreed. If I flip it and nothing happens, I assume it's broken.
That's our show. Go look at your settings screen and judge it kindly.
episodes.summary:
What a settings screen says about how an app sees its users.

• {3} Hiding everything distrusts users; showing everything is indecision.
• {5} Good defaults plus a few self-explaining switches.
• {6} A switch should take effect immediately.

albums.name: Footnotes of History
albums.speaker: eleanor
albums.notes: Short stories from the margins of big history.
albums.profile:
Each episode follows one small object, rule or accident that ended up shaping something much bigger.

No dates to memorise — just the story, and why it still matters.

episodes.title: The Clock That Unified Britain
lines: Hello, and welcome to Footnotes of History. I'm Eleanor Hughes.
Until the eighteen forties, every town in Britain kept its own time, set by the sun over the local church.
Bristol ran about ten minutes behind London. Nobody minded, because nobody travelled fast enough to notice.
Then came the railways. A train leaving London at noon arrived in Bristol at a time that made no sense on either clock.
Passengers missed connections. Worse, two trains on one line could disagree about what time it was.
So the railway companies did something radical. They adopted London time everywhere, and called it railway time.
Towns resisted for years. Some clocks were built with two minute hands, one for local time and one for the railway.
By eighteen eighty, it became law. The whole country set its watches to Greenwich.
So the next time you check your phone, remember: the time on it was invented by a train timetable.
Thanks for listening. Until next time.
episodes.summary:
How railways forced Britain onto a single clock.

• {1} Every town kept local solar time.
• {3} Trains made the differences impossible to ignore.
• {6} Some clocks had two minute hands.
• {7} Greenwich time became law in 1880.

bookmarks.note: Two minute hands! Find a photo of one.

episodes.title: Why Ships Ate Sauerkraut
lines: This is Footnotes of History. Today, a story about cabbage, and the sea.
On long voyages in the seventeen hundreds, scurvy killed more sailors than storms or battles.
Captain James Cook was determined that his crew would not suffer the same fate.
He loaded his ship with barrels of sauerkraut. The problem was, the sailors refused to eat it.
So Cook served it only at the officers' table. Within a week, the crew were demanding their share.
Sauerkraut didn't actually hold much vitamin C after months at sea. Cook's real advantage was fresh food at every port.
But the story of the officers' table is still taught as a lesson in persuasion.
Sometimes the fastest way to make people want something is to tell them they can't have it.
episodes.summary:
Captain Cook, scurvy, and a lesson in persuasion.

• {1} Scurvy killed more sailors than battles.
• {4} Serving sauerkraut only to officers made the crew want it.
• {5} The real cure was fresh food at port.

episodes.title: The Library That Lent Out People
lines: Welcome to Footnotes of History. This week, a library with an unusual catalogue.
In Copenhagen, in the year two thousand, a group of young people set up what they called a human library.
Instead of books, you could borrow a person for thirty minutes and ask them anything.
A police officer. A refugee. Someone living with schizophrenia. Each one a book with a title on its cover.
The idea was simple. It's harder to hold a prejudice against someone once you've sat across a table from them.
Today, human libraries run in more than eighty countries.
It's a small footnote, but a hopeful one. Thanks for listening.
episodes.summary:
A library in Copenhagen that lends out people instead of books.

• {2} Borrow a person for thirty minutes.
• {4} Prejudice is harder face to face.
• {5} Now in more than eighty countries.

albums.name: The Sleep Lab
albums.speaker: priya
albums.notes: Evidence-based answers to the questions you ask at three in the morning.
albums.profile: A sleep researcher and a chronic insomniac go through one sleep question per episode, separating what the evidence says from what the internet says.

episodes.title: Does Melatonin Actually Work?
lines: Welcome to The Sleep Lab. I'm Sam Doyle, and I have not slept well since about two thousand nineteen.
And I'm Doctor Priya Raman. Today's question comes from Sam, unsurprisingly. Does melatonin work?
I take it most nights. Am I wasting my money?
It depends what you're using it for. Melatonin is a timing signal, not a sedative. It tells your body when night is.
For jet lag, or for shifting a late body clock earlier, the evidence is quite good.
And for just falling asleep faster on a normal night?
Modest. Studies find people fall asleep a few minutes sooner on average. Not nothing, but not magic.
Timing matters more than dose. A small amount, a few hours before bed, often beats a big one at bedtime.
So I've been doing it exactly backwards.
Most people are. Next week: is it really bad to look at your phone in bed?
episodes.summary:
Melatonin is a timing signal, not a sleeping pill.

• {3} It tells the body when night is.
• {4} Good evidence for jet lag and late body clocks.
• {6} Only a few minutes faster to fall asleep on a normal night.
• {7} Timing beats dose: small, a few hours before bed.

bookmarks.note: Try 0.5 mg at 8pm instead of 5 mg at 11

episodes.title: Phones in Bed: How Bad Is It?
lines: This is The Sleep Lab. Priya, I'm recording this from bed, on my phone. Judge me.
I'll judge the evidence instead. The blue light story is weaker than most people think.
Screens at normal brightness shift melatonin a little, but the effect on actual sleep is small.
So why do I feel awful after scrolling until midnight?
Because the problem isn't the light. It's the content. Scrolling is designed to keep you awake and engaged.
Something calm, like an audiobook or a familiar podcast, is very different from an endless feed.
So listening to this podcast in bed is fine.
Listening to this podcast in bed is excellent. Set a sleep timer, and goodnight.
episodes.summary:
It's what you look at, not the light.

• {1} The blue light effect is weaker than claimed.
• {4} Engaging content is the real problem.
• {5} Calm audio is fine — use a sleep timer.

albums.name: Slow Money
albums.speaker: arjun
albums.notes: Personal finance for people who'd rather not think about personal finance.
albums.profile: Arjun explains one money habit per episode in plain language — no stock tips, no get-rich-quick, just the boring things that work.

episodes.title: The Three-Account System
lines: Hello and welcome to Slow Money. I'm Arjun Mehta.
Today, the simplest system I know for not worrying about money. Three bank accounts.
Account one is for bills. Rent, utilities, insurance. Everything fixed goes here automatically on payday.
Account two is for spending. Whatever is left for the month, you spend freely, and without guilt.
Account three is for saving. A fixed amount moves there first, before you ever see it.
The trick is that you never have to do arithmetic. If the spending account has money, you can spend it.
It sounds too simple. That's the point. Systems you have to think about are systems you stop using.
That's it for today. Go open two more accounts.
episodes.summary:
Bills, spending and saving — three accounts, no arithmetic.

• {2} Fixed costs leave automatically on payday.
• {3} Spend what's left without guilt.
• {4} Savings move first, before you see them.

bookmarks.note: Systems you have to think about are systems you stop using

episodes.title: Why You Should Pay Yourself First
lines: Welcome back to Slow Money. Last time, three accounts. Today, the most important habit behind them.
Pay yourself first. It means your savings come out of your income before anything else does.
Most people save whatever is left at the end of the month. And at the end of the month, there is nothing left.
Spending expands to fill whatever is available. That's not a character flaw. It's just how people work.
So make the available amount smaller. Automate the transfer for the morning after payday.
Start with five percent if that's all you can do. The habit matters more than the number.
In a year, you'll have a cushion you barely noticed building. That's slow money.
episodes.summary:
Savings come out first, automatically.

• {2} Saving what's left means saving nothing.
• {3} Spending expands to fill what's available.
• {5} Start at five percent; the habit matters most.

episodes.title: 《活着》：苦难里的温柔
lines: 大家好，欢迎收听晚安读书，我是林晓。
今天我们聊余华的小说《活着》。
很多人说这是一本让人流泪的书。主人公福贵失去了几乎所有的亲人。
但我每次重读，记住的却不是苦难，而是他身上那种安静的韧性。
余华说过，人是为活着本身而活着，而不是为了活着之外的任何事物。
这句话听起来很简单，却需要一辈子去理解。
如果你最近觉得很累，不妨读一读这本书。
好了，今天就到这里。晚安。
episodes.summary:
余华《活着》：苦难之下的韧性。

• {2} 福贵几乎失去了所有亲人。
• {3} 重读时记住的是安静的韧性。
• {4} 人是为活着本身而活着。

bookmarks.note: 人是为活着本身而活着

episodes.title: 《小王子》：重要的东西眼睛看不见
lines: 欢迎收听晚安读书。今天这本书，很多人小时候就读过，那就是《小王子》。
小时候读，它是一个童话。长大以后再读，才发现它是写给大人的。
书里的狐狸对小王子说，只有用心才能看清，重要的东西用眼睛是看不见的。
小王子的玫瑰之所以特别，是因为他为她花费了时间。
我们身边的人也是这样。陪伴本身，就是意义。
今晚睡前，想一想你的那朵玫瑰是谁。晚安。
episodes.summary:
《小王子》是写给大人的童话。

• {2} 重要的东西用眼睛是看不见的。
